finalText:
`async` and `defer` both make an external script download in parallel with HTML parsing. They differ in when the script runs and whether order is guaranteed. `async` runs the script as soon as it has arrived, in no guaranteed order. `defer` runs it after parsing finishes, in document order, before `DOMContentLoaded`.

## What each does

**No attribute.** A plain external classic script is fetched and run immediately, and the parser stops until both are done. The spec says: "If neither attribute is present, then the script is fetched and evaluated immediately, blocking parsing until these are both complete." (https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/scripting.html)

**`async`.** For an external classic script, "the classic script will be fetched in parallel to parsing and evaluated as soon as it is available (potentially before parsing completes)." (https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/scripting.html)
- Downloading doesn't block the parser, but execution does interrupt it. MDN says the executing script "blocks the page from rendering" (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/script).
- In the spec's processing model, an async script goes into a "set of scripts that will execute as soon as possible". It is a set, so nothing orders its entries.

**`defer`.** The classic script "will be fetched in parallel and evaluated when the page has finished parsing." (https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/scripting.html)
- The spec appends such scripts to a "list of scripts that will execute when the document has finished parsing", and the parser runs them from that list.
- MDN describes the timing as after the document has been parsed but before `DOMContentLoaded` fires (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/script).

**Both together.** `async` wins. MDN says "the element will act as if only the async attribute is specified." The spec says authors may still write both so that legacy browsers that only know `defer` fall back to deferred behaviour instead of blocking. (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/script and https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/scripting.html)

## Timing relative to DOMContentLoaded

- **`defer` scripts hold up `DOMContentLoaded`.** MDN's event page says it fires once the document is parsed "and all deferred scripts (<script defer src="…"> and <script type="module">) have downloaded and executed." It also says the event "doesn't wait for other things like images, subframes, and async scripts to finish loading." (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Document/DOMContentLoaded_event)
- **The sequence for deferred scripts.** `document.readyState` becomes "interactive" when parsing completes, before the deferred and module scripts run. `DOMContentLoaded` then fires after they finish. (same MDN event page)
- **`async` scripts have no fixed position.** `DOMContentLoaded` doesn't wait for them. An async script that arrives early can run before parsing ends, and so before `DOMContentLoaded`. A slow one runs after it. Code in an async script should check `document.readyState` instead of assuming either case.
- **A difference in wording between the sources.** The spec says an async script may run "potentially before parsing completes". A note on MDN's event page says `DOMContentLoaded` fires "before the execution of scripts with async." The spec's wording is the broader one. Treat the MDN note as describing the common case, not a guarantee.

## Execution order with several scripts

- **`async`: no ordering guarantee.** MDN says "You get no guarantee that scripts will run in any specific order." Its example of three async scripts warns that a script depending on jQuery may run before jQuery has loaded. Use `async` only for independent scripts. (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/script)
- **`defer`: document order.** MDN says "Scripts with the defer attribute will execute in the order in which they appear in the document." This holds even if a later script finishes downloading first, because the spec runs them from an ordered list. (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/script)
- **Dynamically inserted scripts.** Scripts created with `document.createElement` have "force async" set to true, so they behave as async unless you set `script.async = false`. In that case they go into a separate in-order list and run in insertion order, without waiting for parsing to finish. (https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/scripting.html)

## Inline scripts

`async` and `defer` apply only to external classic scripts.
- MDN says that for inline classic scripts the attribute "would have no effect." (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/script)
- A plain inline classic script runs immediately when the parser reaches it, and it blocks parsing. MDN says such scripts "are fetched and executed immediately before the browser continues to parse the page."

## `type="module"` scripts

- **Deferred by default.** The spec says "Otherwise, the module script and its dependencies will be fetched in parallel to parsing and evaluated when the page has finished parsing. (The defer attribute has no effect on module scripts.)" (https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/scripting.html)
- **Same ordered list as `defer`.** In the spec's algorithm, a parser-inserted script goes into the post-parsing ordered list if it "has a defer attribute or el's type is "module"". Module scripts therefore run in document order, before `DOMContentLoaded`, alongside deferred classic scripts. Placement in the document doesn't change this.
- **`async` on modules.** The module and all its dependencies are fetched in parallel and run as soon as they are available, possibly before parsing completes. There is no ordering guarantee, as with async classic scripts.
- **Inline modules are the exception to the inline rule.** The spec's attribute table allows `async` on inline module scripts. Without `async`, an inline module is deferred. With `async`, it goes into the as-soon-as-possible set. Unlike an inline classic script, it never runs synchronously at parse time. The spec says it always waits for a queued task, even when it has no dependencies.
